title: Splitting data honestly
story:
A held-out score is a simulation of deployment. Everything else about splitting follows from taking that sentence literally: the split is good when the simulation resembles the thing being simulated, and the default way of producing one simulates a world in which the rows are interchangeable and the future is drawn from the same urn as the past.

Sometimes that world is real. Often it is not, and then the arithmetic is still correct while the estimate is optimistic. Three cases cover most of it. When predictions will be made forward in time, a random split lets the model learn from the future and be tested on the past — so split along time instead. When the same entity appears in many rows, a patient, a user, a session, a random split puts some of that entity's rows on each side, and the model scores well by recognising the entity rather than the phenomenon — so hold out whole entities. And when rows are duplicated, near-duplicates land on both sides and the test set stops being unseen.

The mechanical half is the ordering. Split first, before anything that learns from data. The guidance is explicit, and its example is the clearest one available: if you normalise by dividing by an average, the average must be the average of the training subset, not the average of all the data, because if the test subset is included in that calculation then information from the test subset is influencing the model. The same applies to imputation, encoding, feature selection and dimensionality reduction. The rule is never to call fit on the test data.

Then there is the question of what happens to a test set that is used repeatedly, and here the usual telling of the evidence is wrong in an interesting way. Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt and Shankar built new test sets for two long-studied benchmarks, following the original creation processes closely, precisely because a decade of intense research raised the danger of overfitting to excessively re-used test sets. Accuracy dropped by 3% to 15% on one and 11% to 14% on the other, which on the larger benchmark amounted to about five years of progress. That result is widely cited as proof that the community had burned its test set through reuse. Its authors concluded the opposite: model accuracies on the new sets tracked their old accuracies along a line of slope greater than one, the ordering of models was essentially preserved, and they attributed the drop to an inability to generalise to slightly harder images rather than to adaptivity.

So the discipline stands on firmer ground than that experiment, and Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold and Roth supply it: approaches to ensuring validity assume a fixed procedure chosen before the data are examined, while real analysis is intrinsically adaptive — new analyses generated from exploration and from the results of previous analyses on the same data. Every decision you make after looking at a held-out score spends a little of that set's ability to tell you the truth. Not because the numbers decay, but because you are now selecting among choices using the very measurement you will report.

problem.name: Held-out evaluation
problem.shape: You need an estimate of how a model will do on data it has not seen, and the only data available is data you already have.
tell: the rows have a time order and the split does not
the same subject, user or device appears in many rows
a preprocessing step was fitted before the split
the held-out score has been consulted many times while making choices
problem.move: Build the split to match deployment. Split along time when predictions run forward, hold out whole entities when entities repeat, deduplicate before splitting rather than after, and place the split before every step that learns from data. Then decide in advance how many times the final held-out set may be consulted, and report that number alongside the score.
problem.invariant: A held-out score estimates deployment only to the extent that the split reproduces the structure of deployment. Correct arithmetic on the wrong partition yields a precise estimate of a situation that will not occur.
problem.breaks: No split addresses distribution shift, because every partition is drawn from data you already have and production data is drawn later, from a slightly different population, through a slightly different process. Rebuilding test sets for two heavily studied benchmarks produced drops of 3% to 15% and 11% to 14%, attributed to harder examples rather than to anything a better split would have caught.

cost.time: grouped and time-based splitting are cheap to implement and expensive in data, since whole periods or whole entities are withheld rather than scattered rows
cost.space: none beyond holding the split definition with the data, so that the same partition can be reproduced
cost.beats: a random split, which is the right answer only when rows are genuinely exchangeable, and which fails silently and upward in every case where they are not

worked.problem: Cross-validation says 0.92 and production says 0.71. Nobody can find a bug in the code. What is wrong?
worked.reasoning:
Because the split simulated a world the model will not be deployed into, and a correct implementation of the wrong simulation produces exactly this — a confident number and no bug to find.

There are three structures that cause it, and the first question is which one applies here.

Time. If predictions are made forward but the split was random, the training data contains rows from after the test rows. The model learns from the future, and in production the future is not available. Anything with a trend, a seasonality or a regime change makes this large, and the fix is to split along time so that everything in training precedes everything in the test period.

Grouping. If the same entity appears in many rows — a patient measured repeatedly, a user with many sessions, a machine with many readings — a random split puts some of each entity's rows on both sides. The model can then score well by recognising the entity rather than learning the phenomenon, and in production it meets entities it has never seen. The fix is to hold out whole entities. Duplicates and near-duplicates are the degenerate case of the same problem, which is why deduplication has to happen before splitting rather than after.

Distribution shift. Production data is drawn later, from a slightly different population, through a slightly different collection process. This one no split can fix, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than pretending a better validation scheme would have caught it — when new test sets were built for two heavily studied benchmarks following the original processes, accuracy fell by 3% to 15% and 11% to 14%, and the authors attributed that to the models' inability to generalise to slightly harder examples rather than to anything about reuse.

The fourth possibility is not the split at all but the reporting. If the held-out score was consulted repeatedly while choosing features, models and hyper-parameters, then it was being used to select rather than to measure, and it is no longer an unbiased estimate of anything. Validity arguments assume a procedure fixed before the data are examined, and real analysis is adaptive by nature.

So diagnostically I would ask, in order: does the data have a time direction, does it have repeated entities, was any preprocessing fitted before the split, and how many times has this test set been looked at. Then I would rebuild the split along whichever structure applies, expect a lower number, and treat that lower number as the one that was true all along.

problem.practice: Take a model you have evaluated and rebuild its split along whichever structure the data actually has — time, entity, or both — then compare the two scores. The difference is what the original split was hiding. Separately, write down how many times you have looked at your final held-out set, and be honest about whether it is still measuring or has started selecting.

beats.broke: A held-out score is a simulation of deployment, and the default way of producing one simulates a world in which the rows are interchangeable and the future is drawn from the same urn as the past.
beats.fix: Build the split to match how the model will be used — along time when predictions run forward, along the entity when the same subject appears many times, and before any step that learns from the data.
beats.cost: An honest split gives a lower number and less data to produce it with, since holding out whole groups or whole periods costs more than holding out scattered rows — and that lower number is the one you can defend.

interview.q: Cross-validation says 0.92 and production says 0.71. Nobody can find a bug in the code. What is wrong?
interview.trap: Continuing to hunt for a coding error, or assuming the test set was worn out by reuse. The arithmetic is usually right and the partition is usually wrong — and the famous test-set-rebuilding experiment concluded the drop it measured was not caused by adaptivity at all.
interview.answer:
Because the split simulated a world the model will not be deployed into. A correct implementation of the wrong simulation gives exactly this: a confident number and no bug to find.

Three structures cause it, and the first job is deciding which applies. Time: if predictions run forward but the split was random, training contains rows from after the test rows, so the model learned from a future that will not be available in production — anything with a trend, a seasonality or a regime change makes that gap large, and the fix is to split so that all training data precedes the test period. Grouping: if the same entity appears many times — a patient measured repeatedly, a user with many sessions — a random split puts its rows on both sides, and the model scores well by recognising the entity rather than learning the phenomenon, then meets unseen entities in production. The fix is to hold out whole entities, and duplicates are the degenerate case, which is why deduplication belongs before the split.

Third is distribution shift, and no split fixes it. I would say that plainly rather than imply a cleverer scheme would have caught it: when researchers built new test sets for two heavily studied benchmarks by following the original creation processes, accuracy fell by 3% to 15% and by 11% to 14%, and they attributed that to the models' inability to generalise to slightly harder examples rather than to test set reuse.

There is a fourth possibility that is not the split at all. If that held-out score was consulted repeatedly while choosing features, models and hyper-parameters, it was being used to select rather than to measure, and it stopped being an unbiased estimate. Validity arguments assume a procedure fixed before the data are examined, while real analysis is adaptive by construction.

So I would ask in order: does the data have a time direction, does it contain repeated entities, was any preprocessing fitted before the split, and how often has this test set been looked at. Then rebuild the split along whichever structure applies, expect a lower number, and treat that lower number as the one that was true the whole time.

takeaway: A split is a simulation of deployment, so a random one is correct only when rows are genuinely exchangeable — and when they are not, the arithmetic stays right while the estimate goes quietly optimistic.
